Daily deep-dive · Day 7

Consensus & Raft

How a group of servers agree on one ordered log — and keep agreeing through crashes and network splits — by electing a temporary leader and committing only what a majority has stored.

01The problem, in plain words

One machine can keep a durable, ordered log (that's Day 4's WAL). But real systems run several copies for fault tolerance — and the instant you have many machines, a hard question appears: how do they agree on a single sequence of events when any server can crash, and the network can drop, delay, or reorder messages at the worst possible moment?

The goal is a replicated state machine: several servers each holding the same log, applying the same operations in the same order, ending in identical states. Achieve that and the servers are interchangeable — any can serve, and if some die the rest carry on with no data loss. So the whole problem reduces to: get a majority of servers to agree on an ordered log, and keep agreeing as servers fail and recover.

Analogy: a committee writing one shared minute-book with no chairperson-for-life and unreliable phone lines. They elect a temporary secretary who proposes each line. A line is only "official" once a majority of members have copied it into their own books — so even if the secretary vanishes or a few members are unreachable, the official record survives and no two factions can write conflicting official versions.

02The load-bearing idea — majority quorums

Raft uses an odd-sized cluster (typically 3 or 5) and requires every important decision to be approved by a majority (2 of 3, 3 of 5). The property that makes everything work:

the overlap principle Any two majorities of the same cluster share at least one server.

That guaranteed overlap is what prevents contradictions. If one majority committed something, any future majority contains at least one server that witnessed it — so the past can't be silently erased. It's also why a 5-node cluster tolerates 2 failures (3 survive = still a majority) and why even sizes are wasteful: 4 nodes tolerate only 1 failure, same as 3, at higher cost.

03Sub-problem 1 — leader election

At any moment one server is the leader; the rest are followers. All writes flow through the leader, so there's a single authority on log order. Time is divided into numbered terms, each with at most one leader.

The leader sends periodic heartbeats to followers.
A follower that hears nothing for a randomized timeout assumes the leader died, increments the term, becomes a candidate, and requests votes.
Each server votes at most once per term. A candidate that wins a majority of votes becomes leader.
Randomized timeouts make simultaneous candidacies unlikely; if a vote does split, the next round's random timeouts break the tie.

04Sub-problem 2 — log replication

The elected leader accepts client commands, appends each to its own log (order fixed here — it's Day 4's WAL, now with an audience), and sends AppendEntries messages so followers append the same entry in the same slot. The commitment rule is the crux:

commit rule An entry is committed only once the leader and a majority of followers have stored it.

Only then is the entry applied to the state machine and considered permanent. If a follower's log has diverged — missed entries, or stale ones from a dead leader — the leader detects the mismatch and overwrites the follower's log to match its own. The leader's log is the source of truth; followers conform to it.

05Sub-problem 3 — safety

Election and replication alone aren't enough; you need a guard so a new leader can't erase already-committed data. The key rule is the election restriction:

election restriction A candidate can only win if its log is at least as up-to-date as the majority that votes for it.

Because any electing majority overlaps with the majority that committed the last entry, that shared server guarantees the winning candidate already holds every committed entry. Committed data therefore survives every leader change — Raft structurally refuses to elect a leader who is missing it.

06The split-brain test — a network partition

Split a 5-node cluster into groups of 3 and 2:

The 3-side has a majority: it elects a leader and keeps committing. The 2-side can never gather 3 votes, so it elects nobody and commits nothing — it just times out repeatedly. When the partition heals, the stalled minority sees a higher term, steps down, and syncs to the majority's log. There is never a moment where both halves commit conflicting entries. Raft chooses consistency over availability: the minority goes dark rather than risk divergence (the CP corner of CAP).

07Key terminology

Replicated state machine
Multiple servers applying the same ordered log of operations, so all reach identical state. Why it matters: it's the goal. Agreement on the log is the whole point — identical logs mean interchangeable servers.
Term
A numbered epoch of time with at most one leader. Terms increase monotonically. Why it matters: terms are Raft's logical clock — a higher term always wins, which is how stale leaders detect they've been replaced.
Leader / follower / candidate
The three roles. One leader per term handles all writes; followers replicate; a candidate is a follower campaigning for votes. Why it matters: funneling writes through one leader gives a single authority on order — no per-entry negotiation.
Quorum / majority
More than half of all configured servers. Required for both election and commit. Why it matters: two majorities always overlap, which is the single fact that makes consensus safe.
Committed entry
A log entry stored on a majority — now permanent and safe to apply. Why it matters: "on the leader" isn't enough; the majority-ack is exactly what makes an entry survive the leader's death.
Election restriction
Voters reject candidates whose logs are less up-to-date than their own. Why it matters: it's the guard that stops a new leader from erasing committed history.

08Where it's used

SystemHow it uses the idea
etcd (Kubernetes)Every k8s cluster stores its state in etcd, which uses Raft — so you run Raft daily without seeing it.
Consul / NomadHashiCorp's service discovery and scheduler replicate their state via Raft.
CockroachDB / TiKVData is sharded into ranges; each range is its own Raft group for scalable, consistent replication.
Kafka (KRaft mode)Replaced the ZooKeeper dependency with built-in Raft for metadata consensus.
Paxos (the ancestor)The older, correct-but-hard-to-follow algorithm Raft was designed to replace for understandability.

09Common confusions

The leader is a lease, not a title. Any server can hold it; it's re-elected freely whenever the current one falters. There's no permanent master.
Majority means of all configured servers, not the reachable ones. Lose too many and the cluster correctly refuses to progress — unavailability is the safe failure, not a bug.
Committed ≠ written to the leader. An entry only on the leader can still be lost if it dies; the majority acknowledgement is what makes it durable.
Raft gives one agreed log, not throughput. It's a coordination primitive capped by the majority round-trip — which is why systems run many small Raft groups rather than one big one.

10One-sentence summary

Raft keeps a cluster agreeing on one ordered log by electing a temporary leader through majority vote, committing an entry only once a majority has stored it, and refusing to elect any leader missing committed data — staying consistent through crashes and splits, unavailable only when no majority survives.
